# Mapachusetts 🌎

**Politics, mapped to where you live.** An interactive 3D globe that shows every
layer of U.S. government covering a spot (country, state, congressional
district, state senate and house districts, county, city or town, school
district, and city wards where open data exists), plus the elections and town
halls that matter there.

- **Find a place 4 ways:** search, **Use my location**, the *Browse by list*
  menus (State → County → City), or just click the globe.
- **See the stack:** a *layer dock* of color-coded chips, each with a glowing
  outline on the map. Hover or click a chip to highlight that boundary.
- **Ballot by layer:** each layer of government has its own section (what it
  does, and the races it decides). Plus an *Events* tab for town halls, meetings
  and voting dates, and an Election Day countdown.
- **Every state, county and city** is reachable. States and counties are real,
  clickable shapes; counties and cities load from the Census the first time you
  open their parent.
- **U.S. only for now.** The world stays on the globe, but only the U.S. is lit
  up; everything else is greyed out and says it isn't available yet.
- **Candidate profiles:** click a candidate on the ballot (or search a name) to
  open a six-tab research profile: *In the News* (cited), *Funding*, *Career*,
  *Issues* (with voting records), *Sources* and *Myths & Facts*. `?candidate=maura-healey`
  is a shareable link.
- **Voting precincts and wards** for any U.S. spot (Census 2020 voting districts).
- **Night / Day** map themes, keyboard friendly (press `/` to search), phone
  layout with a bottom sheet.

> **Real vs. sample data.** Boundaries and districts are real (Census). The
> **Massachusetts 2026 governor and U.S. Senate races are real**: researched
> candidates (Healey, Minogue, Markey, Deaton) with cited news, funding, issues,
> careers, sources and myths, opened from the ballot, the search box or the
> intro. Everything else (other states' races, local offices, events) is a
> **SAMPLE placeholder**, labeled "Sample" in the UI.

## Run it

Static site using ES modules, so serve it over HTTP (not `file://`):

```bash
python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind 127.0.0.1
# open http://localhost:8000
```

> **Keep `--bind 127.0.0.1`.** This folder also holds the Next.js app, whose
> `.env` file contains secret keys (`SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY`). A plain
> `http.server` serves every file here to anyone on your network, `.env`
> included. `.env` is gitignored; just don't expose this folder. For the
> Next.js app itself see the section at the bottom.

Needs internet (map tiles, MapLibre, the Census service and the geocoder load
from public hosts). Geolocation needs a secure context; `localhost` counts,
production needs HTTPS. No API keys anywhere.

## Where does X go? (start here when adding data)

| I want to add or change...                      | Edit this | How |
| ----------------------------------------------- | --------- | --- |
| **Add or update a researched candidate**        | `supabase/seed-data/<slug>.json` (+ `lib/candidate-profiles.ts`), then `python3 scripts/export_candidates.py` | The export script rebuilds `data/political-data.generated.js`. Never edit that file by hand. See "Political data in the globe". |
| **Which candidates are in which race**          | `data/candidates.js` → `RACES` | List candidate slugs per race; names and parties come from the profiles. |
| **Real races / candidates** (your datasets)     | `data/civic.js` → `fetchRacesForPlace(placeId, stack)` | Return `Race` objects (`data/types.js`). Give each a **`kind`** (which layer decides it) and the UI files it under the right layer. Key district races on the ids in `stack` (e.g. `congress:4822`, `school:4819650`). |
| **Real events / town halls**                    | `data/civic.js` → `fetchEventsForPlace(placeId)` | Return `Event` objects. Optional `kind` adds a colored layer tag. |
| **Sample races/events for one place**           | `data/places.js` → that place's `races: []` / `events: []` | Use factories from `data/races.js` / `data/events.js`. Copy Sugar Land (TX) or Medford (MA). |
| A new **layer of government** (e.g. fire district) | `data/kinds.js` + a lookup in `data/census.js` (or `data/local-sources.js`) | `kinds.js` sets its icon, color and the plain-language blurb. |
| **City wards / council districts** for a city   | `data/local-sources.js` | Add one entry (ArcGIS or Socrata URL + field). It shows up automatically. Boston, Chicago and NYC are done. |
| A new **kind of race** (icon, tag)              | `data/races.js` → `CATEGORY_META` | |
| A new **kind of event**                         | `data/events.js` → `EVENT_TYPES` | |
| **Exact field names / shapes**                  | `data/types.js` | JSDoc for `Place`, `Race`, `Event`, `Jurisdiction`, `GeocodeResult`. Point prompts here. |
| **Geocoder** (text search)                      | `js/geocode.js` | Swap `PHOTON_URL`, or self-host Photon. Holds the U.S.-only filter. |
| **Which countries are active** on the globe     | `js/globe.js` → `ACTIVE_COUNTRIES` | ISO alpha-3 codes. Also needs places in `data/places.js` and a wider geocoder filter. |
| **Map colors / themes**                         | `js/globe.js` → `THEMES`; `styles.css` top | |
| **Layer colors** (used everywhere)              | `data/kinds.js` | One color per layer: map outline, dock chip and ballot section share it. |
| **Look and feel**                               | `styles.css`, `index.html` | CSS variables are at the top of `styles.css`. |

### How it fits together

```
 search / GPS / menus / globe click
              │
        js/navigation.js   (which place am I on? + the exact point)
              │
          js/app.js ────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
              │                                                      │
   data/civic.js  (the ONE data seam)                        js/globe.js  js/ui.js
     ├─ geography ─► data/census.js        real boundaries     (map layers)  (dock, ballot,
     │               data/local-sources.js wards, council                     events, menus)
     └─ politics  ─► data/candidates.js    REAL researched races + candidates
                     data/places.js        SAMPLE races + events (everything else)
```

When you land on a place, the app asks the **Census Bureau (TIGERweb)** which
boundaries contain the point, in parallel, and gets back a **stack** of
`Jurisdiction`s. Each one becomes a dock chip, a glowing outline, and a ballot
section. Races are matched to layers by their `kind`.

Races/events attached to a place (in `data/places.js`) are also **inherited by
everything below it**: put a governor race on the state, a mayor race on the
city.

### Districts follow the exact point

A city can span several congressional or legislative districts. The stack is
looked up for the **spot you searched or your GPS position**; for a plain city
click it uses the city's center, and the UI says so.

## Files

```
index.html         Page structure (command bar, browse panel, hero, dossier, dock)
styles.css         All styling (Night/Day tokens at the top)

scripts/
  export_candidates.py  Teammates' candidate data -> data/political-data.generated.js

prototypes/
  ward-layer/      Original Leaflet voting-district map (kept for reference)

js/
  app.js           Entry point: wires everything together
  candidate-sheet.js  Candidate profile sheet (six tabs), ported from the React app
  navigation.js    "Where am I?" state + the exact point + menu choices
  globe.js         MapLibre 3D globe: world shading, clickable shapes, layer outlines, pins
  ui.js            Renders dock, ballot-by-layer, events, countdown, menus, messages
  search.js        Search-as-you-type box (accessible combobox)
  geocode.js       Text search (Photon), U.S.-only filter
  geolocation.js   Browser location, as a promise

data/
  civic.js         THE data seam. Swap sample politics for real data here
  candidates.js    Real candidates + the races they run in (merge logic from lib/candidates.ts)
  political-data.generated.js  GENERATED from the research app's data. Don't edit
  census.js        Census TIGERweb client: stack, boundaries, county/city lists
  local-sources.js City ward / council-district sources (Boston, Chicago, NYC)
  kinds.js         The layers of government: names, icons, colors, explanations
  places.js        Place tree + SAMPLE races/events + lookup helpers
  races.js         Race factories + category tags
  events.js        Event factories + event-type icons/colors
  levels.js        World > Country > State > County > City > District

  types.js         JSDoc reference for every data shape
```

## Good to know

- **Where your data goes (privacy):** the text typed in the search box goes to
  the public geocoder `photon.komoot.io`. The coordinates of a searched spot or
  of the user's location (only when they press *Use my location*) go to the
  U.S. Census Bureau's TIGERweb service, and to the city open-data portals for
  Boston, Chicago and NYC when the point is in those cities. Nothing else leaves
  the browser. The public geocoder is shared and rate-limited, so self-host or
  use a paid one for production.
- **District maps can lag reality.** Boundaries are whatever the Census has
  published (currently the 120th Congress and 2026 legislative districts). Some
  states redrew maps for 2026, so the UI tells people to confirm with their
  local election office. Congressional districts are not guaranteed to match
  the maps used on Election Day.
- **Cities & towns:** in New England-style states (CT, ME, MA, MI, MN, NH, NJ,
  NY, PA, RI, VT, WI) towns come from Census "county subdivisions"; elsewhere,
  from "incorporated places". A spot with no city or town is shown as
  unincorporated, and the county covers it. A city that straddles counties is
  listed under the county holding its center.
- **Map tech:** MapLibre GL JS 6 (ES module from unpkg, version pinned in
  `js/globe.js` and `index.html`). Basemaps: OpenFreeMap (dark and bright).
  Country shading: MapLibre demo tiles. No keys needed.
- **Sample dates** are relative to today so demos never look stale. Election Day
  events use the real dates (Nov 3, 2026 and Nov 7, 2028).
- **Accessibility:** keyboard-friendly search, tabs and menus; visible focus
  rings; 44px+ touch targets; screen-reader labels; reduced-motion support.
  Full WCAG validation still needs testing with assistive technology and an
  accessibility review.
- **Precincts** come from the 2020 Census voting districts, which can be out of
  date (precincts change often). Treat them as a guide and confirm your polling
  place with your local election office. City *council* wards exist only for the
  three cities in `data/local-sources.js`.
- **Not covered yet:** U.S. territories (Puerto Rico, Guam, ...), real races
  outside Massachusetts, and automated tests.

## Political data in the globe

The candidate research app (below) is the **source of truth** for political
data. The globe is a static site with no build step, so it reads a generated
copy:

```
supabase/seed-data/*.json        politician + cited news summary   ┐
lib/candidate-profiles.ts        funding / issues / career / ...   ┴─► python3 scripts/export_candidates.py
                                                                          │
                                                       data/political-data.generated.js
                                                                          │
                           data/candidates.js  (merge by slug, same logic as lib/candidates.ts)
                                  │                          │
                    racesForState("MA") ──► ballot     getCandidate(slug) ──► js/candidate-sheet.js
```

**Add a candidate:** create `supabase/seed-data/<slug>.json` (copy an existing
one), optionally add a curated profile to `lib/candidate-profiles.ts`, run
`python3 scripts/export_candidates.py`, then list the slug in a race in
`RACES` in `data/candidates.js`. The Next.js app picks up the same files
(`node supabase/build-news-seed.mjs` rebuilds its SQL).

**Live data (not wired yet):** the globe reads the exported file, not Supabase,
so news summaries refresh whenever you re-run the export. To read Supabase
live instead, replace the bodies of `fetchRacesForPlace` in `data/civic.js`
with a call to Supabase's REST API using the **anon** key (it is designed to be
public; Row Level Security gives read-only access). Never put the
`service_role` key in browser code.

---

## Candidate research app (Next.js + Supabase)

> From the `politician_pages` / `candidate-search` branches. This is the
> political-data side of the project: candidate profiles, cited news
> summaries and the Supabase database. The globe UI above reads the same
> candidates through `data/candidates.js` (see "Political data in the globe").

A civic research site for Massachusetts candidates: search a candidate to see
cited summaries of their recent news coverage, funding, issue positions, career
history, sources, and common myths.

- **Framework:** Next.js (App Router) — frontend + API in one project
- **Database:** Supabase (Postgres)
- **Hosting:** Vercel (app) + Supabase (database)

### Routes

- `/` — landing page and the candidate research UI (search plus tabs for
  In the News, Funding, Career, Issues, Sources, and Myths & Facts)
- `/?candidate=<slug>` — opens a candidate's profile directly (shareable)
- `/news` — latest stored headlines, linking to the original reporting
- `/politicians/<slug>` — redirects to `/?candidate=<slug>`

### Where the data comes from

Each profile merges two sources by `slug` (see `lib/candidates.ts`):

- **Supabase** — `politicians` (name, office, party, bio, career history) and
  `politician_news_summaries` (AI-written summaries with numbered citations).
- **Curated profiles** — `lib/candidate-profiles.ts`, hand-written funding,
  issue, source, and myth data from the original candidate-search design.
  A profile without a Supabase row still appears in search.

Tabs with no data for a candidate show an empty state instead of hiding.

### Setup

#### 1. Install dependencies

```bash
npm install
```

#### 2. Create the database

In the Supabase dashboard, open **SQL Editor → New query** and run, in order:

1. [`supabase/schema.sql`](supabase/schema.sql) — tables, indexes, Row Level
   Security (public read).
2. [`supabase/news_seed.sql`](supabase/news_seed.sql) — the 2026 statewide
   candidates and their cited news summaries (Oct 10–24, 2026).

`news_seed.sql` is generated from `supabase/seed-data/*.json`. After editing
those files, rebuild it with `node supabase/build-news-seed.mjs`, which also
validates the citations.

#### 3. Environment variables

Values live in `.env` (gitignored):

```
NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL=https://<your-project>.supabase.co
NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY=<anon public key>
SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY=<service_role secret key>
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=<optional; only for npm run summarize>
```

- The URL and anon key are safe to expose to the browser.
- The `service_role` and Anthropic keys are secrets and are only used
  server-side. Never commit them or ship them to the browser.

#### 4. Run locally

```bash
npm run dev
```

Open http://localhost:3000.

### Refreshing the news

- `npm run ingest` — pulls RSS headlines into `articles`.
- `npm run summarize` — fetches article text (kept in memory only), links
  articles to politicians by full name, and writes cited summaries. Needs
  `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`.
- `npm run news` — both, in order.

Only headlines, links, short snippets, and summaries are stored, never full
article text.

### Deploying to Vercel

1. Push this repo to GitHub.
2. In Vercel, import the repo.
3. Add the environment variables above in the Vercel project settings.
4. Deploy.

import { createClient } from "@supabase/supabase-js";

/**
 * Server-side Supabase client.
 *
 * Uses the service_role key, which bypasses Row Level Security.
 * NEVER import this into a client component or expose it to the browser.
 * It is only safe inside server components, route handlers, and server actions.

export function createServerClient() {
  const url = process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL;
  const serviceRoleKey = process.env.SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY;

  if (!url || !serviceRoleKey) {
    throw new Error(
      "Missing Supabase env vars. Set NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL and SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY."
    );
  }

  return createClient(url, serviceRoleKey, {
    auth: { persistSession: false },
  });

import { getNewsSummaries } from "@/lib/articles";
import { CANDIDATE_PROFILES } from "@/lib/candidate-profiles";
import { getAllPoliticians } from "@/lib/politicians";
import type {
  CandidateProfile,
  CandidateView,
  CareerEntry,
  Politician,
  PoliticianNewsSummary,
  ProfileCareerEntry,
} from "@/lib/types";

/** Normalize a year range for matching ("2013–present" ≈ "2013-present"). */
function yearsKey(years: string): string {
  return years
    .replace(/[\u2012-\u2015]/g, "-")
    .replace(/\s+/g, "")
    .toLowerCase();
}

/** First 4-digit year in a period like "1990s-2004", for sorting. */
function startYear(period: string): number {
  const match = /\d{4}/.exec(period);
  return match ? Number(match[0]) : 0;
}

/** Display the same party label for curated and Supabase records. */
function normalizeParty(party: string | null | undefined): string {
  const value = (party ?? "").trim();
  return value.toLowerCase() === "democrat" ? "Democratic" : value;
}

/**
 * Supabase career rows → Career-tab entries, most recent first. Where a
 * curated profile has a role with the same years, its organization and
 * plain-English description are attached. Falls back to the curated career.
 */
function mergeCareer(
  dbCareer: CareerEntry[],
  profileCareer: ProfileCareerEntry[] = []
): ProfileCareerEntry[] {
  if (dbCareer.length === 0) return profileCareer;

  const byYears = new Map(profileCareer.map((e) => [yearsKey(e.years), e]));
  return [...dbCareer]
    .sort((a, b) => startYear(b.period) - startYear(a.period))
    .map((entry) => {
      const match = byYears.get(yearsKey(entry.period));
      return {
        years: entry.period,
        title: entry.role,
        org: match?.org ?? "",
        description: entry.notes ?? match?.description ?? "",
      };
    });
}

function fromProfileOnly(profile: CandidateProfile): CandidateView {
  return {
    slug: profile.slug,
    name: profile.name,
    role: profile.role,
    party: normalizeParty(profile.party),
    bio: null,
    photo: profile.photo ?? null,
    status: profile.status ?? null,
    openSecretsUrl: profile.openSecretsUrl ?? null,
    career: profile.career ?? [],
    funding: profile.funding ?? null,
    opinions: profile.opinions ?? [],
    sources: profile.sources ?? [],
    misconceptions: profile.misconceptions ?? [],
    news: null,
  };
}

function fromPolitician(
  p: Politician,
  profile: CandidateProfile | undefined,
  news: PoliticianNewsSummary | undefined
): CandidateView {
  const dbCareer = Array.isArray(p.career_history) ? p.career_history : [];
  return {
    slug: p.slug,
    name: p.name,
    role: p.current_office ?? profile?.role ?? "",
    party: normalizeParty(p.party ?? profile?.party),
    bio: p.bio,
    photo: profile?.photo ?? null,
    status: profile?.status ?? null,
    openSecretsUrl: profile?.openSecretsUrl ?? null,
    career: mergeCareer(dbCareer, profile?.career),
    funding: profile?.funding ?? null,
    opinions: profile?.opinions ?? [],
    sources: profile?.sources ?? [],
    misconceptions: profile?.misconceptions ?? [],
    news: news ?? null,
  };
}

/**
 * Every candidate the research UI can show: Supabase politicians (with their
 * cited news summaries) merged with curated profiles by slug. If Supabase is
 * unreachable, the curated profiles still render. Server-only.
 */
export async function getCandidates(): Promise<CandidateView[]> {
  const [politicians, summaries] = await Promise.all([
    getAllPoliticians().catch((err: unknown): Politician[] => {
      console.error("Could not load politicians from Supabase:", err);
      return [];
    }),
    getNewsSummaries().catch((err: unknown): PoliticianNewsSummary[] => {
      console.error("Could not load news summaries from Supabase:", err);
      return [];
    }),
  ]);

  const profiles = new Map(CANDIDATE_PROFILES.map((c) => [c.slug, c]));
  const newsByPolitician = new Map(summaries.map((s) => [s.politician_id, s]));

  const views = politicians.map((p) => {
    const profile = profiles.get(p.slug);
    profiles.delete(p.slug);
    return fromPolitician(p, profile, newsByPolitician.get(p.id));
  });

  // Curated profiles that don't have a Supabase row yet.
  for (const profile of profiles.values()) {
    views.push(fromProfileOnly(profile));
  }

  return views.sort((a, b) => a.name.localeCompare(b.name));
}

# Mapachusetts

*Politics, mapped to where you live.*

**Track:** Civic Action

## What it is

Every U.S. address sits inside a stack of governments: the country, a state, a congressional district, state legislative districts, a county, a city or town, a school district, and often a ward and a voting precinct. It's easy to know who your president and governor are. It's much harder to know your state representative, your school district or your ward, even though those offices decide schools, zoning, policing, roads and local taxes. The information exists, but it's scattered across Census files, city GIS portals, campaign finance sites and news coverage.

Mapachusetts brings it together on an interactive 3D globe. Pick any spot in the United States to see every layer of government that covers it, what each one does, what's on the ballot there, and cited research on the candidates.

## How it works

1. **Find a place, four ways.** Search a city, town, neighborhood, county or state (candidate names work in the same box), press **Use my location**, pick State → County → City from **Browse by list**, or click the globe, where states and counties are clickable shapes and cities are pins.
2. **See your layers.** Mapachusetts asks the U.S. Census Bureau, in parallel, which boundaries contain that point. The answer becomes the **layer dock**: one color-coded chip per government, each with a glowing outline on the globe. Hover a chip to highlight its boundary, or click it to zoom there and open its ballot section.
3. **Read the ballot, layer by layer.** The side panel groups races under the layer of government that decides them, from national down to neighborhood, and each section starts with a plain-language explanation of what that layer does. An **Events** tab lists town halls, meetings, hearings, candidate forums and voting dates.
4. **Research the candidates.** Click a candidate on a race card to open a six-tab profile with a shareable link (for example `?candidate=maura-healey`).

## Features

### Map and geography

- A 3D globe (MapLibre GL) with the U.S. lit up and the rest of the world greyed out. Clicking another country explains that it isn't covered yet.
- Every state, county, city and town in the 50 states and DC. County and town lists load from the Census the first time you open their parent.
- Up to ten kinds of layers per spot: country, state, U.S. House district, state senate district, state house district, county, city or town, school district, city council ward or district, and voting precinct.
- Districts follow the exact point. A large city can span several congressional or legislative districts, so lookups use your GPS position or the specific neighborhood you searched. If you only picked a city, the panel says it's using the city's center and suggests using your location instead.
- Real-world edge cases are handled: New England-style towns versus incorporated cities, unincorporated areas (the app explains that the county provides local services), at-large and delegate House seats, and Massachusetts precinct codes ("0306" reads as Ward 3, Precinct 6).
- City wards and council districts from the Boston, Chicago and New York City open-data portals.
- Night and Day map themes, remembered between visits.

### Ballot and events

- Race cards show the office, election date, term and candidates, tagged **✓ Researched** or **Sample**.
- Event cards show the type, date and time ("Tomorrow", "In 5 days"), venue, whether there's an online option, and which layer of government is holding it.
- A countdown to the next general election (November 3, 2026, then November 7, 2028).

### Candidate research profiles

Researched data covers Massachusetts' two 2026 statewide races: **Governor** (Maura Healey, D, vs. Mike Minogue, R) and **U.S. Senate** (Ed Markey, D, vs. John Deaton, R). Elizabeth Warren also has a curated profile, reachable from search. Profiles open from the ballot, the intro screen or the search box, where candidates appear instantly as you type.

- **In the News:** a neutral summary of recent coverage where every sentence carries numbered citations. Click one to jump to the article. Each 2026 candidate's summary cites eight articles published October 10–24, 2026.
- **Funding:** total raised, top industry, small-donor share and a chart of the top contributing industries, linked to OpenSecrets.
- **Career:** bio and a timeline of roles held, plus current status and committee assignments where available.
- **Issues:** 11 topic areas, from healthcare and housing to climate and technology. Each issue expands into an "In plain English" summary, why people are searching it, a position meter, deeper detail and the related vote record.
- **Sources:** every research source tagged by type and by bias rating (Ad Fontes Media, AllSides), so readers can cross-check across the spectrum.
- **Myths & Facts:** widely shared claims, where they come from, what the record shows, and a primary source to check it.

The four 2026 candidates all have cited news, a bio and a career timeline. Funding, Issues and Myths & Facts are filled in for Markey and Warren so far. For the others, those tabs show a clear empty state, and Funding links to FEC.gov, OpenSecrets and OCPF.

### Built to be trusted

- **Real vs. sample is always labeled.** Boundaries are real everywhere. The Massachusetts governor and U.S. Senate races are real and researched. Other races, local offices and events are placeholders for now, marked "Sample" in the UI.
- **Sources are shown.** Each ballot section credits where its boundary came from. The panel notes that some states redrew districts for 2026 and that precinct lines come from the 2020 Census, and asks people to confirm with their local election office.
- **Citations are checked.** The summarizer is told to stay neutral, use only the articles it's given and cite every sentence, and it keeps only citations that actually appear in the text. The seed build fails if a citation points nowhere, a source is never cited, a link isn't HTTPS, or an article falls outside the research window.
- **Nonpartisan design.** Layer colors deliberately avoid red and blue.
- **Respect for publishers.** We store headlines, links, short snippets and summaries, never full article text. Article text is held in memory only while a summary is written.
- **Privacy.** No accounts and no API keys in the browser. Place searches go to the Photon geocoder, and coordinates go to the Census Bureau (plus the Boston, Chicago or NYC portal inside those cities). Your location is read only when you ask for it.

### Accessible by default

- Full keyboard support: `/` or Ctrl/Cmd+K jumps to search; the search box is an accessible combobox (arrow keys, Enter, Escape, screen-reader announcements); tabs follow the standard arrow-key pattern; Escape closes a profile and returns focus where you left off.
- Skip link, visible focus rings, 44px+ touch targets, screen-reader labels, live status messages and reduced-motion support.
- **Browse by list** is a full alternative to the map.
- On phones, the side panel becomes a bottom sheet.
- Plain language throughout. Full WCAG conformance still needs testing with assistive technology and an expert review.

## Architecture: Netlify + Supabase

- **Netlify (frontend).** The globe is a static site: HTML, CSS and vanilla ES modules with no build step. `netlify.toml` publishes only the site's own files (`index.html`, `styles.css`, `js/`, `data/`), so nothing else in the repo is served.
- **Supabase (backend).** Postgres is the system of record for candidate data, in four tables: `politicians`, `articles`, `article_politicians` and `politician_news_summaries`, with full-text and fuzzy name search indexes. Row Level Security makes every table public read-only; writes happen only server-side with the service-role key.
- **News pipeline.** `npm run ingest` pulls RSS headlines into `articles`, de-duplicated by URL. `npm run summarize` fetches each article, matches politicians by full name, links them, and asks Claude for a cited summary that is validated and saved per politician.
- **Candidate research app.** A Next.js (App Router, React 19) site reads Supabase server-side: candidate search with the same six tabs, `?candidate=` deep links, and a `/news` page of stored headlines that link to the original reporting.
- **One source, two apps.** The researched candidate files build both a validated SQL seed for Supabase and a static data module for the globe, and both apps merge the data the same way. The globe ships that snapshot, so it runs on static hosting with no database keys in the browser. The current summaries were researched with Kiro sub-agents and pass the seed build's validation.

### Public data sources

- **U.S. Census Bureau TIGERweb:** states, counties, cities and towns, 120th Congress districts, 2026 state legislative districts, school districts and 2020 voting districts. Free, keyless and queried live from the browser.
- **City open data:** City of Boston Open Data, City of Chicago Data Portal and NYC Open Data for wards and council districts.
- **Maps and search:** OpenStreetMap data via Photon, OpenFreeMap basemaps and MapLibre demo tiles for country shapes.
- **Candidate research:** Massachusetts and national news outlets (The Boston Globe, WBUR, GBH News, WCVB, Boston.com and others), OpenSecrets, Senate and Congress.gov records, GovTrack, Ballotpedia, PolitiFact and FactCheck.org.

## Who it's for and how it grows

Mapachusetts is for anyone who has looked at a ballot and recognized only the top few names: first-time voters, people who just moved, and people who don't follow politics closely. It also helps teachers, organizers and local reporters explain who represents a given block.

The geography already works nationwide, so growth is mostly adding data, and each step is small by design:

- **A city's wards:** one config entry pointing at an ArcGIS or Socrata layer.
- **A candidate:** one JSON file, a re-run of the export script, and a line adding them to a race.
- **A new layer of government** (a fire district, for example): one entry in `data/kinds.js` plus a lookup.
- **Real races for any state:** every ballot item flows through one module (`data/civic.js`), so a statewide feed or the Supabase tables can replace the sample data without touching the UI.

Next up: reading Supabase live from the globe through its public read-only access, running the news pipeline on a schedule, and adding races for more states and the U.S. territories.

## Try it

On the intro screen, pick **Boston, MA** (wards and council districts), **Medford, MA** or **Sugar Land, TX**, or open a candidate under "Massachusetts 2026: meet the candidates." Press **Use my location** to see your own layers.

**Built with:** MapLibre GL JS, vanilla JavaScript, Next.js, React, TypeScript, Supabase (Postgres), Netlify, Python, Node.js, the Anthropic Claude API, U.S. Census TIGERweb, Photon (OpenStreetMap) and OpenFreeMap.
